reasons.reason: KMHFR's data model carries facility-level constituency location and, if reachable, could in principle support constituency facility counts. The Atlas indicator, however, is health facilities assessed per 10,000 residents and requires a population denominator aligned to the current 290-constituency boundary and reference period. The governed P23 census review found no direct current-290 constituency population series or authoritative crosswalk supporting that denominator. A facility count is not relabelled as a population density, and no county/sub-county population is inherited downward. P28A amendment (2026-09-16): this decision's original framing that KMHFR "provides" a usable constituency facility count was never live-verified and is now corrected — direct reachability tests of the KMHFR public portal and its documented API host (run on 2026-09-08 and again on 2026-09-16, eight days apart) both found every connection unreachable (DNS resolves; every TCP handshake over HTTP/HTTPS times out or is refused), while the Ministry's own health.go.ke apex domain responded normally in the same tests, showing this is a targeted, persistent access failure of the KMHFR host rather than a general outage or a one-off blip. No alternative official, current, geocoded/constituency-tagged facility export was found either: the only official KMHFR-derived download on the Humanitarian Data Exchange is a 2017 snapshot with no coordinates that predates and does not reconcile to the 2023 Kenya Health Facility Census total already anchoring this indicator at county level, and the Ministry's own 2023 census report never publishes facility counts below county. So this constituency gap is not solely a denominator problem: the facility-count numerator is also currently blocked at its designated source, on top of the pre-existing, independently confirmed absence of a current-290 constituency population denominator (see the parallel P24 ward-population investigation in data/p24/ward-census-closure-contract.json, which found KNBS's 2019 census tabulates no finer than sub-location and that no gazetted electoral-constituency/ward population count exists). Both inputs remain genuinely unavailable, not merely unintegrated.
reasons.source: Ministry of Health — Kenya Master Health Facility Registry (KMHFR)

reasons.reason: KNBS's 2019 KPHC publication does not publish average household size as a direct current-290-constituency table. County/sub-county values are not inherited, and lower administrative-unit household counts are not aggregated without an authoritative constituency crosswalk; the older KNBS constituency table predates the current 2012-01 constituency configuration. P28A re-audit (2026-09-16) independently re-verified this by downloading and text-extracting KNBS 2019 KPHC Volume II (Distribution of Population by Administrative Units, https://www.knbs.or.ke/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/2019-Kenya-population-and-Housing-Census-Volume-2-Distribution-of-Population-by-Administrative-Units.pdf) in full: its own List of Tables shows Table 2.4 (Distribution of Population by Sex, Number of Households, Land Area, Population Density and Sub Locations) is the finest administrative tier published -- there is no Table 2.x for constituencies. 'Constituency' and 'Ward' appear in Volume II exactly twice, both times as fields on the raw household enumeration questionnaire reproduced in the appendix, not as a published aggregate table -- a census questionnaire field recording constituency does not by itself constitute a published constituency statistic (see rules, above). The re-audit also confirmed KNBS administrative sub-counties (the finest county-nested tier that is aggregated, in Table 2.3) are not the same delineation as the 290 IEBC electoral constituencies and cannot substitute for them without a crosswalk KNBS has not published: e.g. Table 1.2 lists 5 KNBS sub-counties for Kwale County (Kinango, Lunga Lunga, Matuga, Msambweni, Samburu) against Kwale's 4 IEBC constituencies, and 11 KNBS sub-counties for Meru County against Meru's 9 IEBC constituencies. Separately, the re-audit downloaded and text-extracted the older, standalone 'Constituency Population by Sex, Number of Households, Area and Density' publication (https://www.knbs.or.ke/constituency-population-by-sex-number-of-households-area-and-density/, republished 2013) and confirmed it is 2009-census Volume 1B (Population Distribution by Political Units), whose own text states its tables 'are tabulated for the 210 constituencies and the 47 counties in Kenya' -- i.e. it is definitively the pre-2012-delimitation constituency configuration referenced above, not a current-290 table, and using it to derive household size (population / households) would require exactly the unavailable 210-to-290 crosswalk this closure already prohibits inventing. The re-audit also checked the KNBS Kenya National Data Archive (NADA) catalog entry for the 2019 KPHC (https://statistics.knbs.or.ke/nada/index.php/catalog/116); its public study metadata documents no constituency-level geographic identifier or downloadable constituency aggregate and describes geographic coverage only at 'The Whole Country' / household-and-individual microdata level, not a released constituency tabulation. No credible S0-S4 primary or secondary source, and no defensible S1 official-derived computation (an authoritative population figure and an authoritative household-count figure at the same current-290-constituency granularity), was found. As of this re-audit, IEBC has also publicly ruled out any constituency/ward boundary delimitation review before the 2027 general election -- the constitutional March 2024 deadline was missed, and a January 2025 High Court ruling (under appeal) invalidated the underlying 2019 census population figures for Garissa, Wajir and Mandera counties specifically -- so the current 2012-01, 290-constituency boundary remains the operative geography with no imminent republication of constituency-level census tables or a fresh KNBS-IEBC crosswalk in prospect.
reasons.source: KNBS — 2019 Kenya Population and Housing Census Reports

reasons.reason: KNBS's 2019 KPHC publication does not publish population as a direct current-290-constituency table. Published county/sub-county/administrative-unit values are not inherited or cross-walked without an authoritative boundary mapping. P28A re-opened this closure on 2026-09-16 and independently re-verified and substantially extended the original finding rather than grandfathering it: (1) Volume II (Distribution of Population by Administrative Units) was downloaded and its full text inspected directly. Its own table of contents confirms its finest published tiers are Table 2.2 county, Table 2.3 sub-county, Table 2.4 sub-location and Table 2.5 urban centres; the word 'Constituency' occurs only twice in the ~250-page volume, as blank geocoding fields on the reproduced household questionnaire form in the appendix, not as a published statistic — this directly confirms rule 4 below rather than merely asserting it. (2) The separately-linked KNBS page above (legacy_constituency_table_url) was re-examined directly: it does list all 290 constituencies matching the current post-2012 delimitation, but it was published 2013-03-22 and its figures are the 2009 census count, not the 2019 KPHC — independently corroborated by the Humanitarian Data Exchange, which hosts the identical table explicitly titled 'Kenya population per constituency (2009).csv'. This sharpens the prior reason: the disqualifying defect is a census-period/vintage mismatch (2009 count presented as 2019 KPHC data), not solely a boundary mismatch. (3) Kenyan press reporting contemporaneous with the 2019 KPHC release (The Star, 2020-03-01, 'IEBC, KNBS battle over control of crucial data'; Daily Nation, 'Storm brewing over review of constituency boundaries') documents that KNBS compiled an unpublished internal 'Volume V' tabulating 2019 population by constituency and ward for the IEBC delimitation review, but withheld it from public release amid an unresolved inter-agency dispute over electoral-boundary shapefiles; a KNBS official is quoted: 'Unfortunately we cannot release the same without clear boundaries.' Reporters who sought the document directly were unable to obtain it. This Atlas has no access to an unpublished government working document and records this only as evidence that no publicly citable table exists, not as a promotion path. (4) As of 2025-2026 reporting the position has not improved: IEBC confirmed no constituency/ward boundary review will occur before the 2027 general election, citing among other reasons that 'KNBS has yet to clarify whether the 2019 census figures can be used as the legal basis for delimitation'; separately, the Garissa High Court (Petition No. 4 of 2020, Sheikh & 24 Others v KNBS, IEBC & 3 Others, ruling 2025-01-28) invalidated the 2019 KPHC count for Garissa, Wajir and Mandera counties (14 of 290 constituencies) and ordered a fresh census there, with the Court of Appeal (Civil Appeal No. 236 of 2025) since directing that matter remain in status quo pending determination of the appeal. Part of the underlying 2019 county-level count is therefore itself under active, unresolved judicial challenge, independent of the constituency-table publication gap. (5) The P28A secondary/modelled fallback hierarchy was searched exhaustively for a representation opportunity: no third-party aggregator (HDX, OCHA Kenya COD-AB/COD-PS, WorldPop's published country products, Wikipedia) hosts a 2019-vintage current-290-constituency population table; every constituency-level population dataset located, including on HDX, is the 2009 count. OCHA's Kenya COD-AB/COD-PS products stop at ADM2 (sub-county) and are documented as not reconciling to constituency geography. A genuinely modelled S5 fallback (aggregating a WorldPop-style gridded population raster to the Atlas's own existing 2012-01 constituency polygons in data/geography/geometry/constituencies.geojson) was considered, consistent with this programme's modelled-estimate allowance, but this repository currently has no raster/zonal-statistics tooling (no GDAL, rasterio or geotiff dependency), and there is no published constituency-level figure anywhere against which a from-scratch aggregation could be sanity-checked. Building one under this review's time and tooling constraints would risk producing exactly the kind of unverifiable computed figure the Atlas's anti-fabrication standard exists to prevent, so it was not attempted; it remains a legitimate, well-scoped future workstream (see refresh_trigger).
reasons.source: KNBS — 2019 Kenya Population and Housing Census Reports

No authoritative crosswalk exists to aggregate published sub-location (or any coarser KNBS unit) counts into the 1,450 current wards, so no genuine ward-level published figure can be attached without fabricating one. P28A re-opened this closure on 2026-09-16 and found the ward-level gap shares, and compounds, the constituency-level gap documented in data/p23/constituency-census-closure-contract.json: Kenyan press reporting (The Star, 2020-03-01, 'IEBC, KNBS battle over control of crucial data'; Daily Nation, 'Storm brewing over review of constituency boundaries') documents that KNBS compiled an unpublished internal 'Volume V' tabulating 2019 population by constituency AND ward for the IEBC delimitation review, but withheld it amid an unresolved inter-agency dispute over electoral-boundary shapefiles (a KNBS official: 'Unfortunately we cannot release the same without clear boundaries'); no public copy has surfaced since, and as of 2025-2026 reporting IEBC has confirmed no ward boundary review will occur before the 2027 general election, in part because 'KNBS has yet to clarify whether the 2019 census figures can be used as the legal basis for delimitation.' Separately, the Garissa High Court (Petition No. 4 of 2020, ruling 2025-01-28) invalidated the underlying 2019 KPHC count for Garissa, Wajir and Mandera counties, with the Court of Appeal (Civil Appeal No. 236 of 2025) since ordering status quo pending appeal — so even the sub-location counts a future crosswalk might aggregate are, for those three counties, currently under active judicial challenge. reasons.reason: The Atlas attempted to resolve this indicator at ward level via spatial_derivation: a point-in-polygon count of geocoded, operational KMHFR facilities against the Atlas's own canonical 1,450-ward polygon layer (data/geography/geometry/wards.geojson), divided by a ward population denominator. Both the public KMHFR facility portal and its documented GIS/API host were unreachable from the build environment on repeated attempts on 2026-09-08 (DNS resolved; every TCP connection over HTTP and HTTPS timed out or was refused), while the Ministry's own health.go.ke apex domain was reachable at the same time, showing this is a targeted access failure rather than a general outage. A systematic search for a genuine alternative official geocoded facility list found none that qualifies: the only official KMHFR-derived extract available for download (HDX "Kenya - Health facilities in Kenya", 2017) has no latitude/longitude field at all and is a 2017 snapshot of 8,932 facilities that predates and does not reconcile to the 2023 Kenya Health Facility Census total (14,883 facilities) already anchoring this indicator at county level; the only current, geocoded facility datasets found (healthsites.io's "Kenya Healthsites" export and the Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team's "Health Facilities of Kenya" export) are both built from OpenStreetMap volunteer mapping rather than an official government registry and both self-disclose incomplete, geographically uneven coverage, so neither can support a Class C spatially-derived observation under the Atlas data-quality framework, which requires a documented official input for that class. Independently, the ward population denominator required for a facilities-per-10,000-residents rate does not yet exist in the canonical registry (IND-POPULATION currently resolves only to country and county level). A facility count is not relabelled as a population density, and no county or constituency value is inherited downward to any ward. P28A re-verification (2026-09-16): KMHFR and opendata.go.ke remain unreachable eight days later under the identical failure signature, ruling out a transient outage; no new official geocoded facility dataset appeared on HDX (the 2017 KMHFR extract is byte-identical to the one already rejected); and the Ministry's own 2023 Kenya Health Facility Census report — reachable and directly inspected — confirms its underlying microdata captures each facility's ward via the KMHFR-fed field questionnaire, but the published report itself never tabulates facility counts below county level, so it cannot substitute for a live ward-geocoded KMHFR export. A separate, independent P24 investigation into the ward population denominator (data/p24/ward-census-closure-contract.json, indicator IND-POPULATION) found that KNBS's 2019 census tabulates no finer than the sub-location, that Kenya's 1,450 IEBC electoral wards were never gazetted with an official population count, and that no authoritative sub-location-to-ward crosswalk exists — independently confirming the denominator side of this gap is not merely unresearched but genuinely unpublished. Both a reachable geocoded official facility export (the numerator) and an official current-boundary ward population figure (the denominator) remain actual, diligence-backed blockers, not two framings of one problem.

This is the same documented Mandera East/Lafey spatial hold referenced throughout the Atlas (CHANGELOG.md; docs/DATA-COMPLETION-PLAN.md, Track B and the P24 acceptance criteria) and deliberately preserved through the P23A/P23X constituency and ward voter materialisation: the ten source rows remain correctly included in the Mandera East and Lafey constituency-level totals as an exact aggregation of all official First Schedule child-ward rows, but are not force-matched, interpolated, or evenly split across the five ward polygons in either constituency at the ward level. The ward-level completeness ledger slot for these ten wards is therefore closed as boundary unresolved — a genuine geometry/crosswalk constraint distinct from data non-publication — rather than left as an unexplained blank or filled with a fabricated or force-matched value.

reasons.reason: The Kenya Demographic and Health Survey (KDHS) 2022 -- the sole source for Children 12-23 months fully vaccinated with basic antigens at any level in this Atlas (KDHS 2022 Main Report Table 10.4C) -- was itself explicitly designed and powered only to national, urban/rural and county domains of estimation, never to constituency. Its own Key Indicators Report states this directly: "The 2022 KDHS was designed to provide estimates at the national level, for rural and urban areas, and, for some indicators, at the county level" (Kenya Demographic and Health Survey 2022 Key Indicators Report, Section 2.1 "Sample Design", p.3, https://dhsprogram.com/pubs/pdf/PR143/PR143.pdf). The survey's own two-stage stratified design explains why: each of the 47 counties (Nairobi and Mombasa purely urban) was split into 92 rural/urban strata, from which 1,692 clusters were drawn nationally using Equal Probability Systematic Sampling (KDHS 2022 Main Report, Chapter 1 "Sample Design") -- an average of roughly 36 clusters per county, already spread thinly across the ~6 constituencies an average county contains (290 constituencies over 47 counties), so no constituency-level sampling stratum was ever constructed. Neither the Key Indicators Report nor the full Volume I/Volume II final reports publish this indicator, or any indicator, below county level anywhere in their tables. DHS Program's own public geocoded survey-cluster dataset, which could in principle support a transparent spatial join, is deliberately imprecise for exactly this reason: cluster coordinates are randomly displaced up to 2km for urban clusters and up to 5km for rural clusters (with a further randomly-selected 1% of rural clusters displaced up to 10km), restricted only to keep the displaced point inside the country and the original survey region (DHS Spatial Analysis Report 7, "Geographic Displacement Procedure and Georeferenced Data Release Policy for the Demographic and Health Surveys", https://dhsprogram.com/pubs/pdf/SAR7/SAR7.pdf) -- a displacement radius comparable to or larger than many constituencies, which makes reliably assigning an individual cluster to one of Kenya's 290 constituencies unsound even before the underlying sample-size problem is considered.
